g.q: Where ___ your brother work?
g.e: With he/she/it in present simple questions we use does + base verb: Where does he work?

g.q: Which question is correct?
o: What time do you get up?
g.e: Question word order: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb: What time do you get up?

g.q: ___ you go to the market yesterday?
g.e: Yesterday is past, so we use did + base verb: Did you go...?

g.q: Which question is correct?
g.e: With can, we just put can before the subject. We don't use do: Can you swim?

g.q: Where ___ you born? (be)
g.e: Born is always in the past: Where were you born? With you we use were.

g.q: What ___ you do last weekend? (auxiliary verb)
g.e: Last weekend is past. Past simple questions use did + base verb: What did you do?

v.q: I usually ___ my homework after dinner.
v.e: We say do homework, do housework, do exercise.

v.q: Do you ___ TV in the evening?
v.e: We watch TV, films and football. We don't say see TV or look TV.

v.q: Do you ___ a musical instrument?
v.e: We play an instrument: play the guitar, play the piano.

v.q: My dad ___ shopping every Saturday.
v.e: We say go shopping, go swimming, go running (go + -ing activity).

v.q: Do you l___ to music when you study?
v.e: We listen to music. Remember the preposition to after listen.

v.q: I want to l___ a new language this year.
v.e: We learn a language, learn to swim, learn to drive.

s: Where did you go on your last holiday?
Do you usually do your homework after dinner?
What kind of music do you listen to?
Can you play a musical instrument?

g.q: My sister ___ in Palermo.
g.e: With he, she and it, present simple verbs add -s: she lives.

g.q: ___ your brother wear glasses?
g.e: Your brother = he, so the question uses does + base verb: Does he wear...?

g.q: We ___ go to the beach in winter.
g.e: Negative present simple with I/you/we/they: don't + base verb.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: She goes usually to bed late.
She usually goes to bed late.
Usually goes she to bed late.
g.e: Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb (but after be): She usually goes to bed late.

g.q: My grandfather ___ (not drive) any more.
g.e: He/she/it negative: doesn't + base verb (no -s): he doesn't drive.

g.q: Paolo ___ (study) English on Tuesdays.
g.e: Verbs ending in consonant + y change to -ies with he/she/it: study, studies.

v.q: He has long ___ hair.
v.e: Curly describes hair. Tall and slim describe a person's body, not hair.

v.q: Someone who talks a lot is ___.
v.e: Talkative = likes talking a lot. Shy people often don't talk much.

v.q: My cousin never shares his sweets. He's so ___.
v.e: Mean = doesn't like giving or sharing things. The opposite is generous.

v.q: Which word describes appearance, not personality?
v.e: Slim describes how someone looks. Kind, clever and lazy describe character.

v.q: The opposite of hard-working: l___
v.e: A lazy person doesn't like working. The opposite is hard-working.

v.q: My brother is very t___. He's almost two metres!
v.e: We use tall for height. The opposite is short.

s: My best friend is tall and has short dark hair.
She's very friendly but a bit shy at first.
Does your brother look like your dad?
He doesn't talk much, but he's really kind.

g.q: Look! It ___.
g.e: Look! shows it's happening now, so we use the present continuous: be + -ing.

g.q: What ___ you wearing today?
g.e: Present continuous questions: be + subject + -ing. With you we use are.

g.q: I ___ my jacket today because it's cold.
g.e: For actions happening now or today, use am/is/are + -ing. We need am before wearing.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: The negative present continuous is isn't/aren't/'m not + -ing. We don't use doesn't.

g.q: They ___ (sit) on the sofa right now.
g.e: Right now = present continuous. Sit doubles the t: sitting.

g.q: Shh! The baby ___ (sleep).
g.e: The action is happening now, so we use is + sleeping.

v.q: You wear these on your feet:
v.e: Trainers are sports shoes. Gloves go on your hands and shorts on your legs.

v.q: The bank is ___ the pharmacy and the café.
v.e: Between = in the middle of two things. Next needs to (next to), and we don't say on here.

v.q: The bus stop is ___ the school, on the other side of the road.
v.e: Opposite = facing something, on the other side of the road.

v.q: Which one is NOT clothes?
v.e: A sink is in the kitchen or bathroom. You wash things in it, you don't wear it!

v.q: You wear a b___ around your waist to hold up your trousers.
v.e: A belt goes round your waist to keep your trousers up.

v.q: My phone is in the p___ of my jeans.
v.e: A pocket is a small bag in your clothes where you can keep things.

s: I'm wearing jeans and a blue jumper today.
The café is opposite the station, next to the bank.
What are you doing right now?
She's sitting between her brother and her cousin.

g.q: We ___ to Sicily last summer.
g.e: Last summer is finished time, so we use the past simple. Go is irregular: went.

g.q: Did you ___ a good time?
g.e: After did we use the base form of the verb: Did you have...?

g.q: I ___ my passport at the airport!
g.e: Lose is an irregular verb. The past simple is lost, not losed.

g.q: They ___ like the hotel last year.
g.e: Past simple negative: didn't + base verb. Last year tells us it's past.

g.q: We ___ (stay) in a small hotel near the beach.
g.e: Stay is a regular verb, so the past simple adds -ed: stayed.

g.q: I ___ (not buy) any souvenirs.
g.e: Past simple negative: didn't + base verb. Not didn't bought.

v.q: We went ___ in the mountains and slept in a tent.
v.e: Go camping = stay in a tent. Sightseeing is visiting famous places.

v.q: When it's hot, I love lying on the beach and ___.
v.e: Sunbathing = lying in the sun. You can't ski on a hot beach!

v.q: The weather was awful. It was cold and ___.
v.e: Awful weather is bad weather: cold and rainy. Sunny, warm and hot are nice.

v.q: We ___ a hotel room online before the holiday.
v.e: Book a room = reserve it. You don't buy or hire a hotel room.

v.q: go s___ = visit famous places in a city
v.e: Go sightseeing = visit the famous sights (monuments, churches, museums).

v.q: Put clothes in a suitcase before a trip = p___
v.e: We pack a suitcase before we travel. The opposite is unpack.

s: We spent a week at the beach last summer.
Did you go sightseeing in Palermo?
The hotel was lovely but the weather was terrible.
I left my sunglasses at the airport.

g.q: I ___ TV when the phone rang.
g.e: Past continuous for an action in progress when something else happened. With I we use was.

g.q: What ___ you doing at eight last night?
g.e: Past continuous questions: was/were + subject + -ing. With you we use were.

g.q: While I ___ dinner, I burnt my finger.
g.e: While + past continuous for the longer background action.

g.q: They ___ playing football at three o'clock.
g.e: Past continuous negative: wasn't/weren't + -ing. With they we use weren't.

g.q: At midnight I ___ (sleep).
g.e: An action in progress at a time in the past: was/were + -ing.

g.q: At ten o'clock we ___ (not listen) to the teacher. We were chatting!
g.e: An action (not) in progress at a time in the past: weren't + -ing. Look: we were chatting.

v.q: My birthday is ___ March.
v.e: We use in with months, years and seasons: in March, in summer.

v.q: See you ___ Monday!
v.e: We use on with days and dates: on Monday, on the fifth of May.

v.q: I'll meet you ___ the bus stop.
v.e: We use at for a point or place where we meet: at the bus stop, at school.

v.q: My cousin lives ___ Palermo.
v.e: We use in with cities and countries: in Palermo, in Italy.

v.q: The shops close ___ night.
v.e: We say at night, but in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening.

v.q: I was born ___ 2012.
v.e: We use in with years: in 2012.

s: I was having lunch when you called me.
What were you doing when the lights went out?
We were walking on the beach at sunset.
My birthday is in May, on a Friday this year.

g.q: I was tired, ___ I went to bed early.
g.e: So introduces a result: I was tired (reason), so I went to bed (result).

g.q: We stayed at home ___ it was raining.
g.e: Because introduces a reason: why did we stay at home? Because it was raining.

g.q: First we had lunch. ___ we went for a walk.
g.e: Then shows the next action in a story: first... then...

g.q: ___ the film was long, we enjoyed it.
g.e: Although shows a contrast: the film was long, but we still enjoyed it.

g.q: It was a good film, b___ it was too long.
g.e: But connects two contrasting ideas: good, but too long.

g.q: I was having a shower w___ the doorbell rang.
g.e: When introduces the short action that interrupts a longer one.

v.q: Suddenly we ___ a strange noise.
v.e: We hear a noise. Listen needs to and means you try to hear.

v.q: I ___ a text message from my brother.
v.e: We say get a message or receive a message.

v.q: The thief ___ away when he saw the police.
v.e: Run away = escape quickly from someone or something.

v.q: It was dark, so I ___ the light.
v.e: We switch on (or turn on) a light. We open doors and windows.

v.q: When we saw the fire, we c___ the police.
v.e: Call the police = phone them for help.

v.q: I couldn't open the door because I l___ my keys.
v.e: Lost (past of lose) = I couldn't find them. Left (past of leave) = I didn't take them with me.

s: It was late, so we decided to go home.
Suddenly we heard a noise outside the window.
First we had dinner, and then we watched a film.
Although it was cold, we went for a walk.

g.q: Look at those clouds! It's ___ rain.
g.e: We use be going to for predictions when we can see evidence now (the clouds).

g.q: We ___ going to visit my aunt in Catania.
g.e: Be going to: we use are with we, you and they.

g.q: ___ you going to study tonight?
g.e: Questions with going to: be + subject + going to: Are you going to...?

g.q: Be careful! You're going to ___!
g.e: After going to we use the base form of the verb: going to fall.

g.q: She ___ going to buy a new phone. (not)
g.e: Negative: isn't/aren't/'m not + going to. With she we use isn't.

g.q: What ___ they going to do this summer?
g.e: With they we use are: What are they going to do?

v.q: You go through ___ where they check your bags for dangerous things.
v.e: At security they check you and your hand luggage before you fly.

v.q: You wait for your flight in the ___ lounge.
v.e: Departures = leaving. You wait in the departure lounge before your flight.

v.q: After landing, you collect your suitcase at ___.
v.e: Baggage reclaim is where you collect your suitcases after the flight.

v.q: The flight is ___, so we have to wait two more hours.
v.e: Delayed = late. If it's cancelled, there's no flight at all.

v.q: A card that lets you get on the plane: a b___ pass
v.e: A boarding pass shows your seat and gate. Board = get on a plane.

v.q: The plane t___ off at six.
v.e: Take off = leave the ground. The opposite is land.

s: We're going to fly to London next month.
Where are you going to stay in London?
Don't forget your passport and boarding pass.
I think our flight is going to be delayed.

g.q: I ___ my grandparents this Sunday.
g.e: Present continuous for fixed future plans and arrangements: I'm visiting...

g.q: What ___ you doing tomorrow evening?
g.e: To ask about arrangements: What are you doing + future time?

g.q: We're ___ to Rome next weekend.
g.e: Present continuous = be + -ing, even when it's about the future.

g.q: Which sentence is about a future arrangement?
o: I'm meeting Anna at six tomorrow.
g.e: Present continuous + a future time (tomorrow) = an arrangement.

g.q: She ___ (not come) to the lesson tomorrow.
g.e: Negative arrangement: isn't/aren't + -ing.

g.q: They ___ (have) a party on Saturday night.
g.e: A fixed plan: are + having. Have loses the e before -ing.

v.q: We arrived ___ Palermo at midnight.
v.e: Arrive in + city or country; arrive at + building or place. Never arrive to.

v.q: What are you talking ___?
v.e: We say talk about something: What are you talking about?

v.q: I'm waiting ___ the bus.
v.e: We wait for someone or something.

v.q: It depends ___ the weather.
v.e: Depend on, not depend of (dipende da is different in Italian!).

v.q: Can you look a___ my dog this weekend?
v.e: Look after = take care of.

v.q: I often think ___ you.
v.e: We say think about or think of someone.

s: I'm meeting my friends in the town centre tomorrow.
What are you doing this weekend?
We're arriving in Palermo on Friday evening.
Are you waiting for the bus to the beach?

g.q: She's the teacher ___ helped me with my exam.
g.e: We use who (or that) for people.

g.q: This is the café ___ we have breakfast.
g.e: We use where for places.

g.q: A fridge is a thing ___ keeps food cold.
g.e: We use that or which for things. Who is only for people.

g.q: It's a place ___ you can buy fresh fish.
g.e: Where for places: a place where you can do something.

g.q: A chef is a person w___ cooks in a restaurant.
g.e: Who is for people: a person who...

g.q: A library is a place ___ you can borrow books.
g.e: We use where after a place.

v.q: It's ___ kind of fruit. It's yellow and long.
v.e: To explain a word we say It's a kind of... Fruit starts with a consonant sound, so a, not an.

v.q: It's something you use ___ opening bottles.
v.e: Something you use for + -ing, or something you use to + verb.

v.q: It's the ___ of hot. It's cold.
v.e: The opposite of hot is cold. We use this to explain a word we don't know.

v.q: It's ___ a cake, but smaller.
v.e: It's like... = it's similar to. We don't say it's as a cake.

v.q: It's a person who looks after sick people in a hospital: a n___
v.e: A nurse works in a hospital and looks after patients.

v.q: It's something you use t___ cut paper, for example scissors.
v.e: Something you use to + base verb: to cut, to write.

s: It's a place where you can buy fresh fish.
She's the woman who works at the bakery.
It's something you use for cleaning your teeth.
It's the opposite of expensive.

g.q: Have you finished your homework ___?
g.e: We use yet in questions and negatives, at the end of the sentence. Still and just don't go at the end here.

g.q: I've ___ cleaned the kitchen, so don't make it dirty!
g.e: Just = a very short time ago. It goes between have and the past participle.

g.q: She ___ already made her bed.
g.e: Present perfect: has + past participle with he, she and it.

g.q: We haven't done the washing-up ___.
g.e: Yet is used in negative sentences: we haven't done it yet (but we will).

g.q: I ___ (not tidy) my room yet.
g.e: Present perfect negative: haven't + past participle. Tidy becomes tidied.

g.q: He's ___ (already / do) the ironing.
g.e: Already goes before the past participle. Do is irregular: done.

v.q: Can you ___ the bed, please?
v.e: We say make the bed = put the sheets and covers tidy.

v.q: I always ___ the washing on Saturdays.
v.e: We use do for many housework jobs: do the washing, do the ironing.

v.q: Don't ___ a noise, the baby's sleeping!
v.e: We say make a noise, make a mess, make a mistake.

v.q: Who ___ the cooking in your house?
v.e: We say do the cooking, do the shopping, do the washing-up.

v.q: Put the plates in the d___ after dinner.
v.e: A dishwasher is a machine that washes plates, glasses and cutlery.

v.q: Make or do? ___ a mistake
v.e: We say make a mistake, not do a mistake.

s: I've just made my bed and tidied my room.
Have you done the washing-up yet?
My brother has already taken the rubbish out.
Please don't make a mess in the kitchen.

g.q: I ___ a new jacket last Saturday.
g.e: With a finished time (last Saturday) we use the past simple, not the present perfect.

g.q: Have you ever ___ anything online?
g.e: Present perfect = have + past participle. Sell is irregular: sold.

g.q: When ___ you get those trainers?
g.e: Questions with When ask about a specific past time, so we use the past simple.

g.q: Which is correct?
o: I've been to that shop yesterday.
I went to that shop yesterday.
I've go to that shop yesterday.
g.e: Yesterday is a finished time, so we must use the past simple.

g.q: She ___ (never / buy) clothes online.
g.e: Present perfect for life experience: has never + past participle (bought).

g.q: We ___ (go) to the new shopping centre last weekend.
g.e: Last weekend is finished time, so past simple: went.

v.q: Excuse me, where's the ___ room? I want to try on these jeans.
v.e: The fitting room (or changing room) is where you try on clothes in a shop.

v.q: These shoes don't ___ me. They're too small.
v.e: Fit = the right size. Suit = look good on you.

v.q: I'd like to take these back. Can I have a ___?
v.e: A refund is when the shop gives your money back.

v.q: You pay for things at the ___.
v.e: The checkout is where you pay in a supermarket. You put things in a basket or trolley.

v.q: The paper you get after you pay: a r___
v.e: A receipt shows what you bought and how much you paid.

v.q: Can I t___ on this dress?
v.e: Try on = put on clothes to see if they fit.

s: Have you ever bought clothes online?
I bought these trainers at the market last week.
Excuse me, can I try this jacket on?
I'd like a refund, please. Here's my receipt.

g.q: There's ___ at the door. Can you open it?
g.e: We use somebody/something in positive sentences.

g.q: I didn't do ___ at the weekend.
g.e: After a negative verb (didn't) we use anything. Never two negatives in English.

g.q: Is there ___ to eat?
g.e: We normally use anything in questions. Anywhere is for places.

g.q: I can't find my keys ___!
g.e: With a negative verb (can't) we use anywhere. Nowhere would be a double negative.

g.q: N___ called me yesterday. My phone was silent all day.
g.e: Nobody/no one = not one person. It is used with a positive verb (called).

g.q: Let's go s___ different this weekend.
g.e: Somewhere = a place, used in positive sentences.

v.q: The film was really ___. I fell asleep.
v.e: -ing adjectives describe a thing or situation (a boring film). -ed describes how you feel.

v.q: I'm ___ in history.
v.e: -ed adjectives describe feelings: I'm interested in something.

v.q: We were very ___ when we heard the news.
v.e: How we felt = -ed adjective: surprised.

v.q: The weekend was ___. We went to the beach and the zoo!
v.e: The weekend caused the feeling, so we use -ing: exciting.

v.q: After the long walk we were very ___ (tire).
v.e: How we felt = -ed adjective: tired.

v.q: That joke was really ___ (embarrass).
v.e: The joke caused the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective: embarrassing.

s: Did you do anything interesting at the weekend?
Nothing happened, so it was a boring day.
I was so excited that I couldn't sleep.
Is there anybody here who speaks Italian?

g.q: My sister is ___ than me.
g.e: Short adjectives add -er to make the comparative: tall, taller.

g.q: This phone is ___ expensive than that one.
g.e: Long adjectives use more + adjective + than.

g.q: He drives ___ than his brother.
g.e: Drives is a verb, so we need an adverb: more carefully.

g.q: Today isn't ___ hot as yesterday.
g.e: We use as + adjective + as to compare: not as hot as.

g.q: Palermo is ___ (big) than Bagheria.
g.e: One vowel + one consonant: double the consonant and add -er: big, bigger.

g.q: My English is ___ (good) than last year.
g.e: Good is irregular: good, better, the best.

v.q: How do you say 1/2?
v.e: 1/2 = a half or one half.

v.q: How do you say 3.5?
v.e: In English we use a point (.) for decimals and say point, not comma.

v.q: How do you say 50%?
v.e: We say per cent: fifty per cent.

v.q: How do you say 2,500?
v.e: Thousand and hundred have no -s after a number. We use and only before the tens.

v.q: How do you say 1/4? a ___
v.e: 1/4 = a quarter. 3/4 = three quarters.

v.q: How do you say 1/3? one ___
v.e: 1/3 = one third or a third. 2/3 = two thirds.

s: My brother is taller than my dad now.
The train is faster than the bus.
This summer isn't as hot as last summer.
Half the class were late this morning.

g.q: It's the ___ city in Sicily.
g.e: Superlative of short adjectives: the + adjective + -est. Big doubles the g: the biggest.

g.q: That's the ___ film I've ever seen!
g.e: Bad is irregular: bad, worse, the worst.

g.q: What's the most beautiful place you've ___ visited?
g.e: We often use superlative + ever + present perfect: the best I've ever...

g.q: Which is correct?
o: She's the goodest player in the team.
She's the most good player in the team.
She's the best player in the team.
g.e: Good is irregular: good, better, the best.

g.q: It's the ___ (expensive) restaurant in town.
g.e: Long adjectives: the most + adjective.

g.q: This is the ___ (hot) day of the year.
g.e: One vowel + one consonant: double it and add -est: hot, hottest.

v.q: The city centre is very ___. There are always lots of people.
v.e: Crowded = full of people.

v.q: A very small place in the countryside with a few houses is a ___.
v.e: A village is smaller than a town, and a town is smaller than a city.

v.q: There's a lot of traffic and the air is dirty. The city is ___.
v.e: Polluted = the air or water is dirty.

v.q: The ___ is the part of a city with old, historic buildings.
v.e: The old town is the historic centre. The suburbs are outside the centre.

v.q: The opposite of noisy: q___
v.e: Quiet = not much noise. The opposite is noisy.

v.q: There's lots to do at night. The city is very l___.
v.e: Lively = full of life and activity.

s: It's the most beautiful beach I've ever seen.
The old town is lively but very crowded.
What's the best restaurant in your town?
This is the quietest part of the city.

g.q: I don't have ___ time.
g.e: Time is uncountable, so we use much. Many and a few are for countable nouns.

g.q: There are too ___ people on the bus.
g.e: People is countable plural, so too many.

g.q: I'm not old ___ to drive.
g.e: Enough goes after an adjective: old enough.

g.q: This soup is ___ hot. I can't eat it.
g.e: Too + adjective = more than is good: too hot. Too much goes before nouns.

g.q: You don't sleep e___. You need eight hours!
g.e: Enough after a verb = as much as you need.

g.q: Can I have a l___ water, please?
g.e: A little + uncountable noun = a small amount: a little water.

v.q: You use your ___ to smell.
v.e: We smell with our nose, hear with our ears.

v.q: My ___ hurt after the long walk.
v.e: Feet is the plural of foot. We walk on our feet.

v.q: I need to go to the dentist. I've got ___.
v.e: A dentist looks after your teeth, so toothache.

v.q: Your ___ is between your head and your shoulders.
v.e: Your neck joins your head to your body.

v.q: You have ten of these on your hands: f___
v.e: We have five fingers on each hand. On our feet we have toes.

v.q: The part of your leg that bends: k___
v.e: The knee is in the middle of your leg. The k is silent!

s: I don't drink enough water during the day.
There's too much sugar in this cake.
My back hurts because I sit too much.
Are you getting enough sleep at the moment?

g.q: I think it ___ rain tomorrow.
g.e: We use will + base verb for predictions, often after I think.

g.q: Don't worry. You ___ fail the exam.
g.e: Won't (will not) + base verb for a negative prediction.

g.q: ___ they win the match, do you think?
g.e: Question about the future: Will + subject + base verb.

g.q: I don't think she ___ come.
g.e: After I don't think we use will, not won't. The negative is already in don't think.

g.q: You ___ (love) this film, I'm sure.
g.e: Prediction: will + base verb. The short form is 'll.

g.q: It ___ (not be) easy, but we can do it.
g.e: Negative prediction: won't + base verb.

v.q: The opposite of win is ___.
v.e: Win a match; lose a match. Miss is for a bus or train; fail is for exams.

v.q: The opposite of remember is ___.
v.e: Remember and forget are opposites.

v.q: The opposite of push is ___.
v.e: Push a door away from you; pull a door towards you.

v.q: Can you ___ me some money? I'll give it back tomorrow.
v.e: Lend = give for a short time. Borrow = take for a short time. You lend to someone.

v.q: The opposite of pass an exam: f___ an exam
v.e: Pass and fail are opposites.

v.q: The opposite of buy: s___
v.e: Buy and sell are opposites. The past of sell is sold.

s: I think you'll pass the exam easily.
Don't worry, I won't forget your birthday.
Can you lend me your pen, please?
I'm sure our team will win on Sunday.

g.q: It's hot in here. ___ I open the window?
g.e: Shall I...? is used to offer to do something.

g.q: I promise I ___ tell anyone.
g.e: We use will/won't for promises.

g.q: The phone's ringing. Which reply is best?
g.e: We use will for decisions made at the moment of speaking.

g.q: ___ we go to the beach this afternoon? It's a lovely day!
g.e: Shall we...? is used to make a suggestion.

g.q: That bag looks heavy. I ___ (help) you.
g.e: Will for offers: I'll help you.

g.q: S___ I make you a sandwich?
g.e: Shall I...? = an offer. It's more polite than a statement.

v.q: I lent him ten euros and he never paid me ___.
v.e: Pay someone back = return money you borrowed.

v.q: These shoes are too small. I'm going to ___ them back to the shop.
v.e: Take something back = return it to the place you got it.

v.q: What time will you ___ back home tonight?
v.e: Come back = return to a place.

v.q: The soup was cold, so I ___ it back.
v.e: Send back = return food in a restaurant or a thing to a shop because there's a problem.

v.q: Can you g___ me back my book tomorrow?
v.e: Give back = return something to the person who owns it.

v.q: I missed your call. I'll c___ you back tonight.
v.e: Call back = phone someone who phoned you before.

s: Shall I help you with your bags?
I promise I'll give it back tomorrow.
I'll call you back after dinner.
What time will you come back home?

g.q: I ___ a strange dream last night.
g.e: Last night is finished time: past simple. Have is irregular: had.

g.q: What ___ you usually do on Sundays?
g.e: Usually = a habit, so present simple: do + base verb.

g.q: Look! Those boys ___ in the sea.
g.e: Look! = it's happening now, so present continuous.

g.q: I think it ___ sunny tomorrow.
g.e: A prediction about tomorrow: I think + will.

g.q: While I ___ (sleep), the phone rang.
g.e: A longer action in progress in the past: past continuous.

g.q: She ___ (not like) spicy food.
g.e: A general fact about her: present simple negative, doesn't + base verb.

v.q: The film was ___ good. I loved it!
v.e: Incredibly = extremely. I loved it, so the film was very, very good.

v.q: Which is the strongest?
v.e: From weak to strong: a bit, quite, very/really, incredibly.

v.q: Which is correct?
v.e: A bit + adjective, with no of: a bit expensive.

v.q: Which is the weakest?
v.e: A bit = a little. It is weaker than very or really.

v.q: The exam was q___ difficult, but I think I passed.
v.e: Quite = more than a bit but less than very.

v.q: I'm r___ hungry! Let's eat now.
v.e: Really makes an adjective stronger: really hungry = very hungry.

s: I had a really strange dream last night.
The film was incredibly exciting.
I'm quite tired, so I'm going to bed.
What are you doing tomorrow afternoon?

g.q: I went to the market ___ some fruit.
g.e: Use to + infinitive to say why you do something (the purpose).

g.q: It's important ___ water when it's hot.
g.e: After it's + adjective (important, easy, difficult) we use to + infinitive.

g.q: Is there anything ___ in the fridge? I'm hungry.
g.e: After something, anything and nothing we often use to + infinitive: something to eat.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I'm learning English because travel to London.
I'm learning English for to travel to London.
I'm learning English to travel to London.
g.e: For purpose we say to + verb, not for + verb or for to + verb.

g.q: It's easy ___ (make) arancine if you have a good recipe.
g.e: After it's + adjective we use to + infinitive: it's easy to make.

g.q: I've got nothing ___ (do) this weekend.
g.e: After nothing, something and anything we use to + infinitive: nothing to do.

v.q: Don't forget ___ your homework tomorrow.
v.e: Forget is followed by to + infinitive when you talk about something you need to do.

v.q: My brother has decided ___ a new bike.
v.e: Decide is followed by to + infinitive: decide to buy.

v.q: They promised ___ us at the station.
v.e: Promise is followed by to + infinitive: promise to meet.

v.q: We hope ___ Sicily again next summer.
v.e: Hope is followed by to + infinitive: hope to visit.

v.q: I'd like ___ (learn) how to play the guitar.
v.e: Would like is followed by to + infinitive: I'd like to learn.

v.q: She pretended ___ (be) ill so she didn't go to school.
v.e: Pretend is followed by to + infinitive: pretend to be.

s: I went to the park to meet my friends.
It's difficult to learn a new language quickly.
Don't forget to call your grandmother tonight.
We decided to go to the beach on Sunday.

g.q: ___ in the sea is my favourite summer activity.
g.e: When a verb is the subject of a sentence, we use the -ing form: Swimming is fun.

g.q: I'm good at ___ photos.
g.e: After a preposition (at, in, of, for) we use the -ing form: good at taking.

g.q: Thanks for ___ me with my homework.
g.e: For is a preposition, so the next verb takes -ing: thanks for helping.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Read before bed helps me relax.
Reading before bed helps me relax.
To reading before bed helps me relax.
g.e: A verb used as the subject of a sentence takes the -ing form: Reading helps me.

g.q: She's interested in ___ (learn) Spanish.
g.e: After a preposition like in we use the -ing form: interested in learning.

g.q: Before ___ (go) out, check the weather.
g.e: Before and after are prepositions here, so we use -ing: before going.

v.q: I really enjoy ___ to music in the car.
v.e: Enjoy is always followed by the -ing form: enjoy listening.

v.q: Have you finished ___ your room yet?
v.e: Finish is followed by the -ing form: finish tidying.

v.q: My dad doesn't mind ___ the dishes.
v.e: Mind and don't mind are followed by the -ing form: don't mind doing.

v.q: I feel like ___ a pizza tonight.
v.e: Feel like (= want) is followed by the -ing form: feel like having.

v.q: Please stop ___ (talk) and listen to me.
v.e: Stop + -ing means you finish doing an action: stop talking.

v.q: I spend a lot of time ___ (chat) with my friends online.
v.e: Spend time is followed by the -ing form. Chat doubles the t: chatting.

s: I love going to the beach in the summer.
Swimming in the sea makes me really happy.
My sister is very good at drawing animals.
Do you enjoy cooking for your family?

g.q: You ___ use your mobile phone during the exam. It's not allowed.
g.e: Mustn't means it is not allowed. Don't have to means it isn't necessary.

g.q: It's Sunday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early. I can sleep late!
g.e: Don't have to means it isn't necessary, but you can if you want.

g.q: ___ your brother have to wear a uniform at school?
g.e: Have to works like a normal verb. With he, she, it the question uses does.

g.q: My mum is a nurse. She ___ work at night sometimes.
g.e: With he, she, it we say has to. Must is never followed by to.

g.q: Yesterday I ___ (have to) walk home because the bus didn't come.
g.e: Must has no past form, so for the past we use had to.

g.q: Students ___ (must, negative) run in the corridors.
g.e: Mustn't is used for rules: something is not allowed.

v.q: My little brother is afraid ___ the dark.
v.e: We say afraid of something.

v.q: Are you interested ___ history?
v.e: We say interested in something.

v.q: I'm really excited ___ my holiday in London.
v.e: We say excited about something.

v.q: She's very good ___ maths.
v.e: We say good at (or bad at) a subject or activity.

v.q: My parents are very proud ___ me because I passed my exam.
v.e: We say proud of someone or something.

v.q: I'm worried ___ the test tomorrow.
v.e: We say worried about something.

s: You mustn't forget your passport when you travel abroad.
We don't have to wear a uniform at school.
My cousin is afraid of spiders and snakes.
Are you interested in learning to cook?

g.q: You look tired. You ___ go to bed early tonight.
g.e: We use should + verb to give advice. There is no to after should.

g.q: You ___ eat so many sweets. They're bad for your teeth.
g.e: Shouldn't gives negative advice. We never say don't should.

g.q: What ___ I wear to the party?
g.e: In questions, should goes before the subject: What should I wear?

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: Should is the same for all persons (no -s) and is followed by the verb without to.

g.q: You ___ (should, negative) spend all day on your phone.
g.e: Shouldn't + verb means it's not a good idea.

g.q: I don't know what to do. What do you think I s___ do?
g.e: We use should to ask for advice: What do you think I should do?

v.q: What time did you ___ home last night?
v.e: We say get home, with no preposition. We don't say get to home or arrive to home.

v.q: In 'I got an email from my cousin', got means...
v.e: Get + a thing like an email, a letter or a present often means receive.

v.q: In 'It's getting dark', getting means...
v.e: Get + adjective means become: get dark, get cold, get tired.

v.q: My grandparents are ___ old, so they can't walk very far.
v.e: Get + adjective means become: getting old.

v.q: Can you g___ some bread at the supermarket, please?
v.e: Get can mean buy: get some bread.

v.q: My mum always g___ angry when I'm late.
v.e: Get + adjective means become. With she we add -s: gets angry.

s: You should drink more water when it's hot.
I think you shouldn't stay up so late.
What time do you usually get home from school?
It's getting cold, so take a warm jacket.

g.q: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
g.e: In the first conditional, the if part uses the present simple: if it rains.

g.q: If you don't hurry, you ___ the train.
g.e: The result part of the first conditional uses will + verb.

g.q: I'll call you if I ___ time.
g.e: After if we use the present simple, even when we talk about the future.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: If you will study, you will pass.
If you study, you will pass.
If you study, you pass will.
g.e: First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb. No will after if.

g.q: If you eat all that cake, you ___ (feel) sick.
g.e: The result of a possible future situation uses will + verb.

g.q: We won't go to the beach if the weather ___ (not be) good.
g.e: The if part uses the present simple: if the weather isn't good.

v.q: Can you ___ me your pen, please?
v.e: Lend = give something for a short time. Borrow = take something for a short time.

v.q: I ___ my best friend for the first time on my first day at school.
v.e: Meet is for the first time you see someone. Know is when you already know them.

v.q: She ___ a lot of money in her new job.
v.e: You earn money by working. You win a prize or a match.

v.q: You ___ your dad! You have the same eyes.
v.e: Look like + person means you are similar to them in appearance.

v.q: We're w___ for the bus. It's late again.
v.e: Wait for = stay until something arrives. Hope = want something to happen.

v.q: This box is very heavy. Can you help me c___ it?
v.e: Carry = hold something in your hands or bag and take it with you. Wear = have clothes on your body.

s: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
Can I borrow your bike this afternoon?
If you don't study, you won't pass the exam.
My brother earns money working in a restaurant.

g.q: This isn't my bag. It's ___.
g.e: Use a possessive pronoun (mine, yours, hers) without a noun after it.

g.q: Is this pen ___ or mine?
g.e: Yours is a possessive pronoun and replaces your + noun: your pen = yours.

g.q: Their house is big, but ___ is bigger.
g.e: Ours = our house. We use ours when there is no noun after it.

g.q: Whose phone is this? It's ___.
g.e: His is both a possessive adjective and a possessive pronoun: It's his.

g.q: These aren't our seats. ___ (we) are over there.
g.e: The possessive pronoun for we is ours: our seats = ours.

g.q: Is this your jacket? No, it isn't ___ (I).
g.e: The possessive pronoun for I is mine: my jacket = mine.

v.q: She speaks English very ___.
v.e: Good is an adjective. The adverb is well: she speaks well.

v.q: Please drive ___. The road is dangerous.
v.e: Adverbs of manner describe how you do something. Many end in -ly: carefully.

v.q: He ran ___ and won the race.
v.e: Fast is irregular: the adverb is the same as the adjective. Fastly doesn't exist.

v.q: The baby is sleeping, so please talk ___.
v.e: To describe how you talk, use an adverb: quietly.

v.q: My grandfather walks very ___ (slow).
v.e: Add -ly to make an adverb: slow becomes slowly.

v.q: She passed the test ___ (easy).
v.e: For adjectives ending in -y, change y to i and add -ly: easily.

s: Is this umbrella yours or is it mine?
Please speak slowly because I don't understand.
Our flat is small, but theirs is huge.
She plays the piano really beautifully.

g.q: If I ___ a lot of money, I'd travel around the world.
g.e: Second conditional: if + past simple for an imaginary situation.

g.q: If she lived near the beach, she ___ every day.
g.e: The result part of the second conditional uses would + verb.

g.q: What ___ you do if you saw a snake?
g.e: To ask about an imaginary situation, use would: What would you do if...?

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: If I would be you, I'd study more.
If I were you, I'd study more.
If I am you, I'd study more.
g.e: We give advice with If I were you, I'd... No would in the if part.

g.q: If we had a garden, we ___ (get) a dog.
g.e: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb.

g.q: I would go to the party if I ___ (not have) so much homework.
g.e: The if part of the second conditional uses the past simple: if I didn't have.

v.q: A ___ makes honey.
v.e: Bees make honey. Wasps and flies don't.

v.q: Which animal lives in the sea?
v.e: A dolphin is a sea animal. Donkeys live on farms and butterflies fly.

v.q: A ___ has eight legs and makes webs.
v.e: Spiders have eight legs and make webs. Insects have six legs.

v.q: Which one is an insect?
v.e: An ant is an insect with six legs. A bat is a mammal and a snake is a reptile.

v.q: A small insect that bites you at night and makes a noise: m___
v.e: Mosquitoes bite people, especially on summer nights.

v.q: A big black and white animal from China that eats bamboo: p___
v.e: Pandas come from China and eat bamboo.

s: If I saw a shark, I would swim away.
What would you do if a bee stung you?
If I had a pet, I would choose a rabbit.
My sister is terrified of spiders and mosquitoes.

g.q: I've lived in Bagheria ___ 2015.
g.e: Use since with a point in time (2015, Monday, last year).

g.q: We've known each other ___ ten years.
g.e: Use for with a period of time (ten years, two weeks, ages).

g.q: How long ___ you had your dog?
g.e: How long + present perfect asks about something that started in the past and continues now.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: For a situation that started in the past and is still true, use the present perfect, not the present.

g.q: She ___ (be) afraid of the dark since she was a child.
g.e: Present perfect + since for something that started in the past and is still true.

g.q: How long have you ___ (know) your best friend?
g.e: The present perfect uses have + past participle. Know becomes known.

v.q: I'm ___ of flying, so I always take the train.
v.e: Adjectives with -ed describe how you feel: I'm frightened. -ing describes the thing.

v.q: A very strong fear of something is a ___.
v.e: A phobia is a very strong, often irrational fear of something.

v.q: The film was really ___. I couldn't sleep!
v.e: Scary describes the thing that makes you afraid. Scared and terrified describe people.

v.q: I haven't seen my cousins ___ ages.
v.e: For ages means for a very long time. Ages is a period, so we use for.

v.q: I've been at this school s___ September.
v.e: September is a point in time, so we use since.

v.q: Adjective meaning very, very afraid: t___
v.e: Terrified is stronger than scared or afraid.

s: I've been afraid of dogs since I was little.
We have lived in this flat for a long time.
How long have you been interested in music?
My brother has had a phobia of heights for ages.

g.q: She ___ in Palermo in 1998.
g.e: With a finished past time (in 1998) we use the past simple: was born.

g.q: He ___ three books so far, and he's writing another.
g.e: He is still alive and writing, so we use the present perfect for his life until now.

g.q: My grandmother ___ for forty years before she retired.
g.e: The action is finished (she retired), so we use the past simple.

g.q: How long ___ your grandfather work as a teacher? He retired last year.
g.e: He doesn't work any more, so it's a finished period: past simple with did.

g.q: The actor ___ (die) in 2010.
g.e: A finished time in the past (in 2010) needs the past simple.

g.q: I ___ (live) in this town since I was born, and I still love it.
g.e: Since + a situation that continues now = present perfect.

v.q: He ___ school at eighteen and went to university.
v.e: Leave school means finish going to school.

v.q: When people stop working because they are old, they ___.
v.e: Retire = stop working at the end of your career, usually when you're older.

v.q: They ___ married in 2005 and had two children.
v.e: We say get married. The past is got married.

v.q: My family ___ to Milan when I was five, but we came back later.
v.e: Move (to a place) = go to live in a different place.

v.q: She was b___ in a small village near Palermo.
v.e: We say be born: I was born, she was born.

v.q: He went to university and g___ in 2019.
v.e: Graduate = finish university and get your degree.

s: My grandfather was born in a small village.
She has written many songs, but this is her best.
They got married and moved to the city.
Have you ever met a famous person?

g.q: The cat jumped ___ the wall into the garden.
g.e: Over = from one side to the other, going above something.

g.q: We walked ___ the bridge to the other side of the river.
g.e: Across = from one side to the other of a flat surface, like a bridge or a road.

g.q: The ball went ___ the goalkeeper's legs.
g.e: Through = in one side and out of the other, like a tunnel or between legs.

g.q: She ran ___ the hill and was very tired at the top.
g.e: Up = from a lower place to a higher place. She arrived at the top.

g.q: He got ___ the car and walked to the door. (opposite of into)
g.e: Out of is the opposite of into: get into a car, get out of a car.

g.q: The train went t___ a long tunnel.
g.e: We go through a tunnel: in one end and out of the other.

v.q: In tennis, you hit the ball ___ the net.
v.e: In tennis, the ball must go over the net, not into it.

v.q: Which sport do you play on a court?
v.e: We play basketball and tennis on a court. Golf is on a course and skiing on slopes.

v.q: The player kicked the ball and ___ a goal.
v.e: We say score a goal. You win a match.

v.q: In football, the person who stops the ball going into the goal is the ___.
v.e: The goalkeeper stands in the goal and stops the ball.

v.q: The person who controls a football match and makes sure players follow the rules: r___
v.e: The referee controls the match and can give yellow and red cards.

v.q: Our team didn't win or lose. It was a d___.
v.e: A draw is when both teams have the same score.

s: The player ran towards the goal and scored.
We walked along the beach to the harbour.
The ball went over the net and out.
She jumped into the pool and swam across it.

g.q: Your coat is on the floor. Please pick ___.
g.e: With separable phrasal verbs, a pronoun (it, them) goes between the verb and the particle.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: Pronouns go in the middle: turn it off, not turn off it.

g.q: I'm looking ___. Have you seen my keys?
g.e: Look for can't be separated. The pronoun goes after for: look for them.

g.q: Can you look after my dog this weekend? Yes, ___
g.e: Look after can't be separated, so the pronoun goes at the end: look after it.

g.q: These are your shoes. Put ___ (them, on) before we go out.
g.e: With a pronoun, separable phrasal verbs split: put them on.

g.q: The music is too loud. Please turn ___ (it, down).
g.e: A pronoun goes between the verb and the particle: turn it down.

v.q: I usually ___ at seven o'clock on school days.
v.e: Wake up = stop sleeping.

v.q: Can you ___ this word in the dictionary?
v.e: Look up = find information in a dictionary or online.

v.q: Please ___ your mobile phone in the cinema.
v.e: Turn off = stop a machine working.

v.q: I ___ chocolate for a month, but then I started eating it again!
v.e: Give up = stop doing or having something.

v.q: It's cold. P___ on your jumper.
v.e: Put on = start wearing clothes.

v.q: We need to leave now. H___ up!
v.e: Hurry up = do something more quickly.

s: I wake up early, but I get up late.
Please turn it off before you go to bed.
Can you look after my cat this weekend?
I've given up sugar in my coffee.

g.q: The Colosseum ___ by the Romans.
g.e: Past passive: was/were + past participle. Build becomes built.

g.q: English ___ all over the world.
g.e: The language doesn't speak; people speak it. Use the passive: is + past participle.

g.q: Arancine ___ with rice.
g.e: Arancine is a plural noun, so the present passive is are + past participle: are made.

g.q: The telephone was invented ___ Alexander Graham Bell.
g.e: In a passive sentence we use by to say who did the action.

g.q: This bridge ___ (build) in 1920.
g.e: Past passive: was + past participle.

g.q: A lot of oranges ___ (grow) in Sicily.
g.e: Present passive with a plural subject: are + past participle.

v.q: People from Spain are ___.
v.e: The nationality adjective for Spain is Spanish. Nationalities start with a capital letter.

v.q: A person from Switzerland is ___.
v.e: Switzerland: Swiss. Swedish is for Sweden.

v.q: People from the Netherlands are ___.
v.e: People from the Netherlands (Holland) are Dutch.

v.q: A person from Greece is ___.
v.e: Greece is the country and Greek is the nationality.

v.q: A person from China is ___.
v.e: Many nationalities end in -ese: Chinese, Japanese, Portuguese.

v.q: People from France are ___.
v.e: France: French. It's irregular, so learn it!

s: Pizza was invented in Italy, not in America.
This song was written by a famous French singer.
Oranges and lemons are grown all over Sicily.
My neighbours are Portuguese and they speak Italian well.

g.q: When I was little, I ___ hate vegetables.
g.e: Used to + verb talks about past habits or states that are not true now.

g.q: ___ you use to walk to school?
g.e: Questions with used to: Did + subject + use to + verb.

g.q: She didn't ___ like maths, but now she loves it.
g.e: After didn't we write use to, without -d.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: We use to live in Rome.
We used to live in Rome.
g.e: In positive sentences it's used to + verb.

g.q: My grandad ___ (use to) play football every Sunday when he was young.
g.e: Positive sentences: used to + verb, for a past habit.

g.q: I ___ (not / use to) wear glasses.
g.e: Negative: didn't use to + verb. After didn't there's no -d.

v.q: In ___ you learn about countries, rivers and mountains.
v.e: Geography is the study of the Earth, countries and places.

v.q: In ___ you learn about the past.
v.e: History is the study of past events.

v.q: In ___ you study plants and animals.
v.e: Biology is the science of living things.

v.q: You use computers and learn to code in ___.
v.e: ICT means information and communication technology.

v.q: The subject where you do sport at school: P___
v.e: PE means physical education: sport and exercise at school.

v.q: The subject about numbers and equations: m___
v.e: In British English we say maths.

s: I used to be really bad at maths.
Did you use to wear a uniform at school?
My favourite subject was always history.
We didn't use to have computers in class.

g.q: Take an umbrella. It ___ rain later.
g.e: Might + verb means maybe. It never takes -s or to.

g.q: I'm not sure, but I ___ go to the beach tomorrow.
g.e: Use might + verb (no to) for a possibility in the future.

g.q: She ___ come to the party. She has an exam the next day.
g.e: The negative is might not + verb. We don't use do or does with might.

g.q: Which sentence means 'maybe I will go'?
g.e: Might shows the action is possible but not certain.

g.q: Don't touch the dog. It ___ (might, negative) be friendly.
g.e: Might not + verb = maybe not.

g.q: We m___ buy a new car next year, but we haven't decided.
g.e: Might is used when we haven't decided or aren't sure.

v.q: Which is the noun from 'decide'?
v.e: Verbs ending in -de often make nouns with -sion: decide, decision.

v.q: Thank you for the ___ to your party.
v.e: Invite becomes invitation, with -ation.

v.q: Money doesn't always bring ___.
v.e: We make nouns from some adjectives with -ness: happy, happiness.

v.q: There has been a big ___ in your English!
v.e: Improve becomes the noun improvement, with -ment.

v.q: It was a difficult ___ (choose). I liked both jackets.
v.e: The noun from choose is choice.

v.q: We had a long ___ (discuss) about our holiday plans.
v.e: Discuss becomes the noun discussion, with -ion.

s: I might go to the cinema this evening.
It might rain, so take your umbrella.
That was the best decision I've ever made.
My teacher noticed a big improvement in my writing.

g.q: I love pizza. ___ do I.
g.e: To agree with a positive sentence, use So + auxiliary + I.

g.q: I don't like horror films. ___ do I.
g.e: To agree with a negative sentence, use Neither + auxiliary + I.

g.q: I'm tired. So ___ I.
g.e: Use the same auxiliary as the first sentence. I'm = I am, so: So am I.

g.q: I can't swim. Neither ___ I.
g.e: After neither the verb is positive: Neither can I.

g.q: I went to the beach yesterday. So ___ I.
g.e: Past simple positive uses did: So did I.

g.q: I haven't finished my homework. Neither ___ I.
g.e: The present perfect uses have, and after neither it's positive: Neither have I.

v.q: My sister and I have a lot in ___. We like the same music.
v.e: Have a lot in common = share many interests or qualities.

v.q: Your bag is ___ mine!
v.e: We say the same as.

v.q: My brother is very different ___ me.
v.e: Careful! In British English we say different from or different to, not different of or at.

v.q: ___ my parents are teachers.
v.e: Both is used for two people or things.

v.q: The twins are very a___. You can't tell them apart.
v.e: Alike = very similar. It comes after the verb: they are alike.

v.q: Your phone is s___ to mine, but it's a different colour.
v.e: Similar to = almost the same as.

s: I don't like getting up early. Neither do I.
My cousin and I have a lot in common.
I love the sea. So do I!
Your jacket is very similar to mine.

g.q: When we arrived at the cinema, the film ___.
g.e: The past perfect (had + past participle) shows an action happened before another past action.

g.q: I was hungry because I ___ breakfast.
g.e: Not having breakfast happened before I was hungry, so we use the past perfect.

g.q: She ___ never seen the sea before she came to Sicily.
g.e: Before she came is past, so we use had + past participle.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: When I got home, my mum has cooked dinner.
When I got home, my mum had cooked dinner.
When I had got home, my mum has cooked dinner.
g.e: The cooking happened first, so it's in the past perfect: had cooked.

g.q: By the time the police arrived, the thief ___ (escape).
g.e: The thief escaped before the police arrived, so use the past perfect.

g.q: I ___ (not / finish) my homework when my friends called.
g.e: Negative past perfect: hadn't + past participle.

v.q: I waited ___ the rain stopped, then I went out.
v.e: Until = up to the moment when something happens.

v.q: ___ I got to the station, the train had left.
v.e: By the time = when I got there, it was already too late.

v.q: We were watching TV when ___ all the lights went out.
v.e: Suddenly = quickly and unexpectedly.

v.q: Call me ___ you arrive, so I know you're safe.
v.e: As soon as = immediately when something happens.

v.q: We looked for the keys for hours, and e___ we found them in the car.
v.e: Eventually = in the end, after a long time.

v.q: A few minutes l___, the bus arrived.
v.e: A few minutes later = after a few minutes.

s: When I got to school, the lesson had already started.
I had never tried sushi before last summer.
As soon as I got home, I went to bed.
Suddenly, we realised we had forgotten the tickets.

g.q: 'I'm tired.' Yesterday evening, Anna said she ___ tired.
g.e: In reported speech the present usually moves back to the past: am becomes was.

g.q: 'I'll call you tomorrow.' Last week, Marco said he ___ call me the next day.
g.e: In reported speech will becomes would.

g.q: 'I can't swim.' Last summer, Luca told us he ___ swim.
g.e: In reported speech can becomes could, and can't becomes couldn't.

g.q: 'I like chocolate.' Which reported sentence is correct?
o: She said me that she liked chocolate.
She said that she liked chocolate.
She said that she like chocolate.
g.e: Say has no person after it, and the present moves back: like becomes liked.

g.q: 'I don't understand.' Yesterday, Marta said she ___ (not understand).
g.e: Present simple becomes past simple in reported speech: don't becomes didn't.

g.q: 'I'm going to study.' Last night, he said he ___ (be) going to study.
g.e: Am going to becomes was going to in reported speech.

v.q: She ___ me a funny story.
v.e: We tell someone a story. Tell is followed by a person.

v.q: What did he ___ to you?
v.e: We say something to someone. After did we use the base form.

v.q: Don't ___ lies!
v.e: Tell is used with lies, the truth, a story and a joke.

v.q: He ___ that he was sorry.
v.e: Say doesn't need a person after it. Tell needs one: he told me.

v.q: Can you t___ me the time, please?
v.e: Tell + person: tell me the time.

v.q: My grandma always ___ (say / tell) good morning to everyone.
v.e: We say good morning, hello, goodbye. With she we add -s: says.

s: She told me that she was very tired.
He said he would call me later.
Please tell me the truth about what happened.
They said they were going to the beach.

g.q: Who ___ the Mona Lisa?
g.e: When who is the subject of the question, we don't use did: Who painted it?

g.q: What ___ at the end of the film?
g.e: What is the subject here, so there is no auxiliary: What happened?

g.q: Which question is correct?
g.e: Who is the subject, so no did. Win is irregular: won.

g.q: Who ___ you call last night? I called my aunt.
g.e: Here who is the object (you called someone), so we need the auxiliary did.

g.q: Which team ___ (win) the World Cup in 2006? Italy!
g.e: Which team is the subject, so no auxiliary: Which team won?

g.q: How many people ___ (live) in your flat? Four.
g.e: How many people is the subject, so no do: How many people live there?

v.q: ___ is your birthday? In March.
v.e: When asks about time.

v.q: ___ does it cost? Ten euros.
v.e: How much asks about price or uncountable quantity.

v.q: ___ bag is this? It's mine.
v.e: Whose asks who something belongs to. Who's means who is.

v.q: ___ do you go to the gym? Twice a week.
v.e: How often asks about frequency.

v.q: H___ f___ is it from Bagheria to Palermo? About fifteen kilometres.
v.e: How far asks about distance.

v.q: ___ did you leave early? Because I felt ill.
v.e: Why asks for a reason. The answer often starts with because.

s: Who wrote the most famous book you know?
What happened at the party last night?
How often do you go swimming in the summer?
Whose idea was it to come here?
